quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The bookshop on Canal Street has a sign that says 'Sit, read, stay as long as you like.' Armchairs stand between the shelves, and a kettle is always warm for anyone who asks. Owners of other shops once warned that people would read whole books and leave without paying. Some do, but the same customers often return on payday, and many bring friends who then buy gifts. The owner says the armchairs have paid for themselves several times over.
options: How Generosity Turned Readers into Customers
Why Shop Owners Worry About Free Reading
Warm Kettles for Anyone Who Asks
quests.correctAnswer: How Generosity Turned Readers into Customers
quests.hint: The owner's final remark is about money. What does it say about the free reading?
quests.explanation: The armchairs and the kettle are the offer, and the warnings are the opposing view. The passage's point is what the offer produced.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice combines the welcoming policy with the loyal, spending customers that result.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When Amir arrived in the country at fifteen, he spoke almost no English and sat alone at lunch. A boy from his class noticed the way he juggled a soccer ball and invited him to the Saturday game. Nobody needed to explain the rules or the shouting. By the end of the term, Amir had learned the English words for 'pass,' 'shoot,' and 'nice one,' and he had started talking about more than football.
options: Juggling a Soccer Ball at Lunchtime Alone
Moving to a New Country at Fifteen
A Game That Helped a Newcomer
quests.correctAnswer: A Game That Helped a Newcomer
quests.hint: Ask what the game gave Amir beyond the words he learned.
quests.explanation: Vocabulary is one result, and moving country is the background. The story follows Amir from loneliness to belonging through the game.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title shows how the soccer game led from isolation to friendship and conversation.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: At the end of a country lane, a wooden stand holds jars of honey, a tin for coins, and a handwritten price list. Nobody watches over it. The beekeeper, who lives half a kilometer away, says that in eleven years only a handful of jars have vanished, while extra coins are sometimes left with notes of thanks. He believes people behave the way they are expected to.
options: Why a Few Jars Still Go Missing
quests.correctAnswer: Trust at a Roadside Stand
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence is the beekeeper's belief. How do the other details support it?
quests.explanation: Honey, bees, and missing jars are all part of the scene. The unwatched stand and the extra coins show what the beekeeper's belief rests on.
quests.whyThisTitle: It reflects the reliance on people's honesty that the whole arrangement depends on.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: On the hillside estate, tea leaves for the finest grade are still picked by hand. Machines could do the job in a fraction of the time, but they cut everything at the same height and cannot tell a young bud from a coarse leaf. The pickers, mostly women who learned from their mothers, take only the top two leaves and a bud. The higher price the tea earns pays their wages and keeps the tradition alive.
options: Grading Tea by Price at Auction
quests.correctAnswer: The Survival of Hand-Picking
quests.hint: Ask what advantage the human pickers have over the machines, and what it earns.
quests.explanation: The machines, the mothers, and the price are all mentioned. The passage's point links the quality of hand-picked leaves to the reason the method survives.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title reflects the reasons hand-picking continues despite faster machines.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Whales communicate across great distances with low calls that can travel for hundreds of kilometers. Modern shipping has filled the ocean with engine noise in the same range of sound. Researchers who monitor the water report that some whales now call louder or more often, while others seem to fall silent. The concern is not only that they are disturbed, but that they may no longer hear each other.
options: Why Ship Engines Are So Loud
How Ship Noise Threatens Whale Communication
quests.correctAnswer: How Ship Noise Threatens Whale Communication
quests.hint: Look at how the final sentence gives the real concern. What is it?
quests.explanation: Whale calls, engines, and monitoring are three separate elements. The passage joins them into a single concern about lost communication.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title joins the whales' calls and the ships' noise into the passage's concern.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The founders spent two years building an app for splitting restaurant bills. On launch day, few people downloaded it. When they asked users why, the answer surprised them: friends already used a shared note on their phones, and it took ten seconds. The team closed the app, but the lesson stayed with them. Their next product began with a conversation, not a design.
options: Designing Apps for Two Full Years
Lessons a Failed App Taught Its Founders
quests.correctAnswer: Lessons a Failed App Taught Its Founders
quests.hint: Look at how their approach changes at the end.
quests.explanation: The bill-splitting idea and the closure are events. The final sentences show what the founders took away from the failure.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice captures the lesson that changed how the founders began their next product.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When the department store closed, the mall's upper floor sat empty for three years. Then the city moved a school there, since classrooms could be built quickly inside the wide, bright spaces. Students eat lunch in the food court and use the old cinema for assemblies. Parents worried at first, but attendance has improved, and nearby shops now have customers again.
options: Giving an Empty Mall a New Purpose
Eating Lunch in the Food Court
quests.correctAnswer: Giving an Empty Mall a New Purpose
quests.hint: Ask what happened to the space and to the area around it.
quests.explanation: The food court and the closing are pieces of the story. The passage shows an unused space becoming useful, with benefits beyond the school.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title names the transformation from empty space to school and its wider benefit.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The jar of bubbling dough in Mrs. Petrova's kitchen is more than eighty years old. She received it from her aunt, who received it from a neighbor, and each owner has fed it flour and water every day. When she bakes, she keeps a spoonful and gives another to whoever asks. There are now starters descended from hers in kitchens in six countries.
options: A Sourdough Starter Passed from Hand to Hand
Saving a Spoonful for the Next Loaf
Feeding the Dough Every Single Day for Decades
quests.correctAnswer: A Sourdough Starter Passed from Hand to Hand
quests.hint: Follow the jar's history and its future. What connects them?
quests.explanation: Feeding, saving a spoonful, and the six countries are aspects of one story. The passage centers on how the starter travels from person to person.
quests.whyThisTitle: It reflects the chain of owners and the way the starter keeps spreading.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Instead of choosing equipment from a catalog, the town asked local children to draw the playground they wanted. The drawings showed a treehouse, a very long slide, and, in nearly every one, a place to sit and talk. Designers were surprised by the last request. The finished playground has the slide and the treehouse, but the benches under the trees are what teenagers use most.
options: A Very Long Slide for Everyone
quests.correctAnswer: Children as Playground Designers
quests.hint: Consider what the town did differently and what it learned.
quests.explanation: The slide and the benches are outcomes. The passage's main line is the decision to involve children in the design, which produced a surprise.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title names the town's approach, which produced the unexpected request.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Airline pilots with thousands of hours of experience still read from a checklist before every takeoff. They do not do so because they forget how to fly, but because routine tasks are the easiest to skip when the mind is elsewhere. Hospitals that adopted similar lists for surgery saw fewer complications. The list does not replace skill; it protects skill from the ordinary slips of a busy day.
options: Forgetting How to Fly After Years of Practice
Why Experts Still Rely on Checklists
quests.correctAnswer: Why Experts Still Rely on Checklists
quests.hint: The passage gives two fields as examples. What do they share?
quests.explanation: Pilots and hospitals are examples of one point. The last sentence generalizes: checklists guard skilled people against small slips.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title expresses the general idea that the pilots and hospitals both illustrate.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A learner who hears 'it's a piece of cake' may look around for dessert. Idioms mean something different from their individual words, and each language has its own. Translating them word for word usually produces nonsense or a laugh. Interpreters therefore look for an expression in the other language with a similar meaning, even when the images are completely different.
options: Why Idioms Cannot Be Translated Word for Word
quests.correctAnswer: Why Idioms Cannot Be Translated Word for Word
quests.hint: Ask what problem the passage explains and what its answer is.
quests.explanation: The dessert joke opens the passage, and interpreters appear as part of the solution. The passage's core is the problem with literal translation.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice states the problem and the reason the passage explains.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The bench outside the post office has a small brass plate, worn smooth: 'For anyone who needs a rest.' Nobody in town knows who placed it. Delivery drivers eat sandwiches there, and older residents stop to rest halfway through their errands. Last year, when the council proposed removing it for a new bike rack, so many people objected that a rack was added beside it instead.
options: A Bench the Town Refused to Lose
A Plate Worn Smooth by Time
Adding a Bike Rack at the Post Office
quests.correctAnswer: A Bench the Town Refused to Lose
quests.hint: Which event in the passage shows how much people value the bench?
quests.explanation: The drivers, the plate, and the rack are all details. The objection to removing the bench shows the community's attachment.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title reflects the outcome that showed how much residents cared.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: By the time the last runner turned into the stadium, most of the crowd had gone home. The clock read almost seven hours, yet the volunteers still lined the final stretch, and they clapped as if it were the first hour. The runner, a man in his seventies, crossed the line with his arms raised. Organizers say it is often this finish, not the winner's, that makes people cry.
options: Running a Race in Old Age
Celebrating the Last Finisher of a Marathon
Winning a Marathon in Record Time
quests.correctAnswer: Celebrating the Last Finisher of a Marathon
quests.hint: The last sentence contrasts two kinds of ending. Ask which one the passage dwells on.
quests.explanation: The runner's age and the volunteers' hours are details. The passage highlights the emotion of the final finish rather than the winner.
quests.whyThisTitle: It reflects the focus on the last runner and the way people respond to him.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The office fern had been dying for weeks. Everyone noticed the brown leaves; everyone assumed someone else would water it. In a meeting about workplace tasks, a manager mentioned the plant, and nobody claimed it. When the plant finally died, several people felt oddly guilty. The story became a joke, but it also led the team to assign clear owners to every shared job.
options: Caring for Plants in Shared Offices
Running Better Team Meetings Each Week
Feeling Guilty About a Dying Fern
When Everyone's Job Is No One's
quests.correctAnswer: When Everyone's Job Is No One's
quests.hint: Notice how the fern becomes a lesson by the final sentence.
quests.explanation: The fern and the guilt are the story's surface. The changed practice at the end shows what the team took from it.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title expresses the principle the fern's fate demonstrated and the team acted upon.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Two buildings on Linden Road shared a small parking lot, and arguments over spaces were constant. A resident finally created a group chat where drivers post when they leave and when they will return. The chat now handles most requests within minutes. Notes on windshields have disappeared, and residents say they know each other's names for the first time.
options: Learning Neighbors' Names for the First Time
How a Group Chat Ended Parking Disputes
quests.correctAnswer: How a Group Chat Ended Parking Disputes
quests.hint: Which title includes both the problem and the tool that solved it?
quests.explanation: Windshield notes, the parking lot, and neighbors' names are pieces of the story. The passage's arc runs from conflict to a chat-based solution.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title links the constant arguments to the group chat that resolved them.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A teacher gave her students two jars, one labeled 'needs' and one labeled 'wants,' and asked them to sort a week of pocket money into them. At first, the 'wants' jar was full; after a few weeks, several students began moving coins the other way, to save for something bigger. The exercise did not lecture them about money. It simply made each choice visible.
options: Why Children Spend Their Pocket Money Too Quickly
quests.correctAnswer: Making Spending Visible with Jars
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence explains why the exercise worked. What does it say?
quests.explanation: The labels are the setup, and lectures are what the exercise avoided. The passage's point is how the jars changed students' decisions.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice names the method and the effect that the final sentence describes.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Every May, ropes hang down the sides of the old iron bridge and painters begin at the north end. By October they reach the south end, and then they start again; visitors joke that the job never finishes. The engineers see it differently: paint is what keeps the iron from rusting, and a bridge that is painted continuously is never in need of major repair.
options: Why Painting Never Stops on the Old Bridge
Hanging Ropes from the Sides of Iron Bridges
The Joke Visitors Like to Make
quests.correctAnswer: Why Painting Never Stops on the Old Bridge
quests.hint: Consider the difference between the visitors' view and the engineers' view.
quests.explanation: The ropes and the joke are part of the scene. The engineers' explanation reveals why the work is done in a cycle.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title turns the seemingly endless job into a deliberate way of protecting the bridge.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When conservators examined a small portrait with X-rays, they found a different face beneath the visible one. The painter had begun a portrait of an older man, abandoned it, and painted over it. Cracks in the top layer let traces of the first image show through. The discovery does not change the beauty of the finished painting, but it suggests how often artists change their minds.
options: A Hidden Portrait Beneath a Painting
Cracks in the Top Layer of an Old Oil Painting
quests.correctAnswer: A Hidden Portrait Beneath a Painting
quests.hint: Which title covers what was found, not just how it was found?
quests.explanation: X-rays and cracks are the means of discovery. The artists' changes of mind are what the discovery hints at, not the discovery itself.
quests.whyThisTitle: It names the discovery that the whole passage describes.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The farmers of the plain first opposed the wind turbines, fearing they would ruin the fields. Yet the towers occupy only a small patch of ground at each base, and crops grow right up to them. Rent from the turbines gives each family a steady income even in years of poor harvest. Some who objected now ask whether more towers can be built on their land.
quests.correctAnswer: How Turbines Won Over Farmers
quests.hint: Compare the farmers' first reaction with their later one.
quests.explanation: Crops and rent are reasons for the change, and the fears describe the starting point. The passage traces the shift in the farmers' attitude.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title captures the change from opposition to interest, and the reasons for it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: At a remote mountain station, the nearest shop is two hours away. A local baker installed a machine that sells fresh bread, cheese, and boiled eggs, restocked each morning. Hikers arriving after a long climb often say it is the best meal of the trip. The machine also serves residents, who no longer need to drive down for basics.
options: Living Two Hours from the Nearest Shop
A Vending Machine That Serves a Remote Station
quests.correctAnswer: A Vending Machine That Serves a Remote Station
quests.hint: Ask who uses the machine and why it matters there.
quests.explanation: Baking, hiking, and distance are details around the machine. The passage explains how one machine meets the needs of both hikers and residents.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title combines the machine with the two groups it serves in a place far from shops.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In his first week at the supermarket, Daniel was afraid of the customers who complained. By the third week, he realized that most of them were not angry at him but at the price of eggs or the length of the queue. He began listening before answering, and to his surprise, angry faces often softened. He says the job taught him more about people than any class.
options: Daniel's Lessons from His First Job
Why Customers Get Angry in Queues
quests.correctAnswer: Daniel's Lessons from His First Job
quests.hint: Read Daniel's own summary in the final sentence.
quests.explanation: The eggs, the checkout, and the queues form the setting. Daniel's comment in the last sentence shows the passage is about what he learned.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice reflects the growth in his understanding of people that the passage describes.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Chef Amara tastes every dish three times: when the ingredients go into the pan, when the sauce thickens, and just before the plate leaves the kitchen. Younger cooks find this excessive; she says flavors change quickly, and a dish that was perfect a minute ago may not be now. The habit rarely takes more than a few seconds. What it prevents is the small mistake a customer will never forget.
quests.correctAnswer: The Chef Who Keeps Tasting
quests.hint: Consider why the chef defends a habit her colleagues find excessive.
quests.explanation: Sauces, young cooks, and customers all appear in her explanation. The passage is about the reason for the habit.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title represents the chef's reasoning about the repeated tasting.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: On the wall of the old town hall, a series of lines is painted at different heights, each with a date. The highest is well above a person's head. Newcomers often ask what they mean. Locals explain that they mark the floods of the past two centuries, and that the town now builds no homes below the lowest line. The paint is a reminder that memory can protect a place.
options: The Age of the Old Town Hall
Painted Lines That Keep a Town's Flood Memory
quests.correctAnswer: Painted Lines That Keep a Town's Flood Memory
quests.hint: Which detail tells you how the lines are used, and not just what they show?
quests.explanation: The town hall, the building rule, and the newcomers are parts of the account. The final sentence points to the purpose of the marks.
quests.whyThisTitle: It combines what the lines record with the protection that remembering provides.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In the village of Oakhurst, home internet is slow and often fails. So the library added a room with a fast connection, and the community hall began offering a weekly help desk. Now farmers file forms there, students attend online classes, and older residents video-call their families. The room is busy from morning to evening, and people who never spoke before are chatting in the queue.
options: Filing Forms Online from a Village
A Shared Internet Room Brings a Village Together
quests.correctAnswer: A Shared Internet Room Brings a Village Together
quests.hint: Look at how the last sentence adds a benefit that was not the original goal. What is it?
quests.explanation: Forms, calls, and slow internet are pieces of the story. The final point about neighbors chatting shows the wider effect of the shared room.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title covers both the solution to the internet problem and the community ties that grew from it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A local historian posted a photograph of Station Road taken in 1925, then stood in the same place and took another. The buildings on the left are still there; the horses are gone, and so are the shop signs. What surprised viewers was what stayed the same: the curve of the road and the tree at the corner. Hundreds of people have since sent in their own pairs of pictures.
options: The Same Street Across a Century
A Local Historian Taking Photographs of Streets
quests.correctAnswer: The Same Street Across a Century
quests.hint: Ask what the two photographs are being used to show.
quests.explanation: The horses, the historian, and the tree are individual details. The passage is about the comparison and what it reveals about change and continuity.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title reflects the paired photographs showing both what has changed and what has not.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: On the day Mrs. Ito retired, she found her desk covered in letters. Former students, some now in their fifties, wrote about small things: a comment on an essay, a book lent during a hard year, the way she learned every name on the first day. None mentioned test scores. Mrs. Ito said she had spent years worrying about results, and it was only now she saw what people remembered.
options: A Retirement Day Full of Letters and Surprises
Students' Strongest Memories of a Teacher
quests.correctAnswer: Students' Strongest Memories of a Teacher
quests.hint: Which detail tells you what the letters did not include?
quests.explanation: The retirement and names are part of the scene. The absence of test scores, and her reflection, shows what the passage stresses.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice reflects the contrast between the small kindnesses students recalled and the results she worried about.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: On an island with steep valleys, shepherds long ago developed a whistled version of their spoken language. A whistle can carry across a ravine that would take an hour to walk around, so news and warnings passed easily from farm to farm. Roads and phones reduced its use, but the island's schools now teach it, and children practice in class. The whistle is no longer needed for distance; it is a way to keep a heritage.
options: A Whistled Language Finds New Use
quests.correctAnswer: A Whistled Language Finds New Use
quests.hint: The last sentence compares an old purpose with a new one. What are they?
quests.explanation: The valleys and the shepherds explain the original need. The schools and the final sentence show a different reason for keeping the whistle.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title joins the original use of the whistle with the reason it survives today.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The clock tower keeper climbs 212 steps every Monday to wind the mechanism by hand. An electric motor could do it in minutes, and the town has offered to pay for one. He declines politely. The climb is how he notices worn gears and loose bolts before they cause trouble, and the townspeople, he says, would soon stop looking up if the clock never needed anyone.
options: Offering an Electric Motor to a Town
quests.correctAnswer: Winding the Clock by Hand
quests.hint: Ask what the keeper values that a motor could not provide.
quests.explanation: The steps, the motor, and the gears are all mentioned. The passage stitches them into the keeper's reasons for refusing.
quests.whyThisTitle: It reflects the keeper's reasons for choosing the hand-winding over the motor.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In some rail systems, a train that leaves twenty seconds early triggers an official apology. To a traveler used to long delays, this may sound absurd, but when millions of commuters plan their mornings to the minute, twenty seconds can mean a missed connection. The apology is a small sign of how seriously the railway treats the trust that its timetable creates.
options: Planning a Commute to the Minute
quests.correctAnswer: Apologizing for Twenty Seconds
quests.hint: How does the passage move from an odd fact to an explanation?
quests.explanation: Missed connections and planning are reasons given in the middle. The opening puzzle and the closing point about trust are what the passage is really about.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title names the surprising practice and the seriousness about timetables behind it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Elevators in older buildings often have mirrors, and few people ask why. When elevators were slow, riders became impatient and complained. Building managers found that, with a mirror to check their appearance or watch other passengers discreetly, people felt the wait was shorter. The elevators did not speed up; the perception of waiting changed.
options: Checking Your Appearance in a Public Space
quests.correctAnswer: How Mirrors Shorten Elevator Waits
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence contrasts speed with perception. Which one changed?
quests.explanation: Slow elevators and complaints are the problem. The mirror's effect on how the wait feels is the passage's main point.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title shows how the mirrors changed the feeling of the wait even though the speed stayed the same.
